issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Pregnancy/birth reminders are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner in this 34-year-old male unless there is unreported trauma content involving pregnancy, childbirth, or infants. The other trigger items point toward sexualized/interpersonal threat and hospital-associated reminders, making this item the clearest trauma-incongruent outlier.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Locks: repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows
issues.explanation: Repeated lock-checking is more suggestive of fear of external intrusion/burglary than trauma-specific coping with partner physical abuse, and it is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. The other maladaptive strategies reflect interpersonal avoidance and affect suppression, whereas this item introduces a different safety concern.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: This threat item duplicates compulsive checking behavior rather than describing a perceived current threat state, and it implies fear of break-in/external danger that is not otherwise supported by the trauma narrative, appraisals, or memory content. In combination with the matching maladaptive strategy item, it forms an internally coherent pair but one that is poorly integrated with the rest of the formulation.

vignette:
Kwame was thirty-four when his girlfriend Denise beat him so badly that he ended up in the emergency room, choking on his own blood. He had never told anyone she hit him-the shame was too much-but that night, as she pinned him to the floor and screamed accusations he no longer tried to follow, he tasted copper and heard the wet sound of his own breathing. In the hospital, the antiseptic smell burned his nose, and when a male nurse looked at him with what felt like a clinical, almost hungry gaze, Kwame felt a deep wrongness that he could not name.

Back at work as a parole officer, the smell of hand sanitizer in the intake room would immediately put his body on alert-shoulders bunching, fists tightening-and at the same time, the metallic taste of that night would flood his mouth, the screaming ringing in his ears, making the memory feel as if it were happening right now. When a male parolee locked eyes with him during an interview, Kwame felt objectified all over again, his mind racing with the injustice: She got away with it, no one ever held her accountable, and now my life is destroyed. He began avoiding eye contact, dropping his gaze whenever someone looked at him too long, and he started steering clear of any conversation that could turn into a disagreement, even with his current partner, Maria. Positive emotions felt dangerous too-when Maria touched his arm affectionately, he pulled away, because the brief warmth only reminded him that happiness could be ripped away.

After months of this, Kwame had come to believe that the abuse had ruined him permanently. He sometimes caught himself thinking that life was not worth living anymore. That belief made him even more vigilant: every glance from a man, every unexpected smell, every flicker of tension in a room felt like confirmation that the world was still unsafe and that nothing had been put right. The memory kept pushing its way in-the taste of blood, her voice in his head-and each time it did, his body snapped into a state of urgent readiness, his eyes scanning every corner, watching for the next threat. The scanning itself triggered new memories: a parolee's sudden movement would conjure the sound of her fist hitting the floor beside his head.

The more he avoided-the averted eyes, the silent retreats from conflict, the refusal to let himself feel joy-the more the memories intruded, as if his own mind were punishing him for trying to shut down. And the more the memories came, the more convinced he became that his life had no future, which made him avoid every possible confrontation with Maria, leaving her confused and him isolated. His body stayed on alert all the time, and that constant tension fed both the feeling that danger was imminent and the memory of the night when danger had been real. He began to interpret even a neutral look from a male colleague as a sexual assessment, the trigger snapping him straight back into the injustice of it all.

Eventually, Kwame's avoidance cost him a promotion-his supervisor noted he was "too withdrawn" during team meetings-and Maria told him she felt like she was living with a ghost. What finally brought him to a therapist's office was the morning he caught himself thinking, for the third time that week, that it might be easier not to wake up. He was terrified that if he opened up, he would only confirm that his life was indeed over, but he was even more afraid of what might happen if he did nothing.
